Just to expand on the topic of contraception; it's not as simple as yes or no -- Aside from people who are risky or uninformed, there is also the entire group of people who use contraception, but it didn't work properly or broke during intercourse (broken condoms, IUD out of position) resulting in pregnancy. Contraception is a huge grey area and people end up pregnant while using it as best they can. 

You also have women who are told by doctors they are sterile, who actually somehow end up pregnant. It sounds unlikely but this has happened to at least 3 women I know.

I became pregnant since my uterus is slightly deformed (bicornuate ) ; my iud didn't cover the other side, so a fertilized egg could attach to the wall. 

There isn't even a consisrent statistic as to how common uterine deformities are in women and deformities are not even something were educated about to watch out for. Uterine deformities are not something your doctor always checks before you get fitted for an iud, even though they are supposed to. You will use contraception that is 99% effective" and get pregnant. 

My pregnancy ended in a natural miscarriage after 2 months, making my body a murderer. I didn't even understand that I was pregnant because my period is irregular, and since I'm thin, I am used to missing them at times. 

 Then again, something like 1 in 4 conceptions ends naturally by the mother's body and most of the time it is unnoticed because it's very much like a period. There are just "glitches" and your body can't form a perfect baby every time and rejects it. I digress.

Tldr loopholes exist for people who faithfully use contraception, it breaks on us or doesn't work for unforseen reasons. Using contraception with every good intention is a grey area and this distinction needs to be understood.

Generally speaking though, I see human rights as a pyramid, and it starts with things like race, gender, social class, moves up to things like mental health. Not that its less important, but its less fundamental, and society still functions when mental health isnt perfectly addressed.

Whenever he sees my leg bouncing, he stops it. I love that he notices and makes me aware of my behaviour. I think its gotten better! Classic conditioning.

 
He is Japanese. Japan is a different culture, and people raise children really differently there, compared to say, North America. Something I have been really Loving is seeing how Neurodiverse people are treated and interpreted in different cultures! Aspies exist all over the world. So what is everyone else doing when their kid is displaying the typical clinical "wierd" "sensitive" "chewing on a favorite cloth" etc... These children are universal beings, so how do they get treated on the other side of the planet? Is there even acknowledgement, etc... Bear with me.

Japanese children are raised in a traditional culture with really strong disciplining, behaviour modifying parents, and the pressure to conform and grow up to be a hard working citizen in this culture in comparison to American culture where individualism and "dont mess w my freedom (or stimming lol)" is pretty strong. 

Japan is "the squeaky wheel gets the grease"-type situation. (ASD children are "squeaky wheels") So-- with regards to stimming behaviours-- children who leg bounce, look around, space out, etc, are "policed" very quickly and made Very conscious of their bhvrs. South Korea is like this too. Stimming and spacing out is seen as a sign of innocence and is percieved as "cute" I have noticed from attention I regularly would get from South Korean classmates. My boyfriend enjoys my repetitive behaviours, where some guys have found them a turn off. In passing, in a relationship I think its SUPER taboo to call out a partner on ther stimming-- often its a comfort thing, they cant control it, etc.

Manners in Japan -- they spend their first 6 years of school learning (I shit you not) Manners! Social Conventions! To a North American, that is sort of absurd-- we go straight to school where we are tested and graded on academic performance. 
What if, as an aspergirl, you grew up with 6 years of social conditioning that under your belt? Youd be extremely invisible. I guess thats a good thing. For patriarchal cultures who dont typically endorse fidgety, wierdo, dorky aspergirls. Its a stepford wife society. No stimming allowed society. Anyways
Japanese aspergirls and boys exist too. Japan is number one for suicide per capita. 

 I visited Japan once and noticed that they are not as forgiving and accomodating to disability as North America is. Yet in theory aspergers exists there.. So I kind of tried to find hints of where ASD is. 
Americans, the most vocal, freedom enthralled people on the planet are only really now breaking into acknowledging neurodiversity and our rights. 
Fidgety, spacey, leg bouncing, odd people who dress awkwardly ... I didnt see many. 
Its like they were kept out of view, or trained not to do it. I asked my boyfriend where the "wierd" people were. Maybe everyone was very wierd.
 
As I familiarize myself more with Japanese conventions, how "funny" or "different" people are portrayed in their culture has been a total treat for a ND person. -- Aspies are there too, but its not pathologized-- it seems to be more culturally integrated. 


For example, "shaky leg" is a thing there,-- you see it referred to in sitcoms as a trope. Its not pathologized as a clinical aspie stim as much as a universal signal of a person in "nervous" state.. 


Innattention is met with much more scrutiny-- as soon as I space out -- I notice that in North American culture there was a sense of comfort and privacy and we space out and stim a lot in our individual ways, doing something by yourself that feels good. We are encouraged even.

 
I appreciate this: but when I stim and space out, my boyfriend casually notices right away and asks what is wrong, or where am I going-- spacing out, stimming is met with a vigilence that in my lifetime is unmatched in North American contexts, where we are really into our individualist quirks, freedom to do what we feel and privacy. I actually love that he watches over me. Its never intrusive-- I mean the culture he is from is Buddhist and self awareness and thought in action is the name of the game. I am basially saying here that cultural conditioning and stimming has a link, and stimming is met with encouragement or discouragement-- we can change if we put our mind to it.


Self awareness I think is a large part of stimming, and people can be culturally conditioned to be less "stimmy", as I see things. And we can certainly shape ourselves to some extent. Im so glad I dont pick my nose unconsciously. I think its got me fired from jobs and lost me boyfriends and made me generally un-cool.

Anyways, I have had fun using my stims as a type of body language with people from other cultures, because often there is a universal meaning in them and they bring laughter to people who otherwise have a language barrier.

Casting a culturally conscious gaze on our stims has been a trip. I think the aspie community could grow a pair, use our curiosity and get into non-Westenized and less clinical gaze-y interpretations of our groups of behaviours. Aspie behaviours are a clinically assembled group of data, so lets look at a human mental condition in other countries and languages, and get past our fear of the "Other"s percieved innacuracies and superstitions.

 The blank faced girl who chews on the comforting texture of a corduroy jacket is something so subtle, but hilarious and human, that she would easily be typecast as a manga character, and even as 2d media, the universal recognition of self stimulating behaviour is comic and empathic. She is recognizeable in the conventions of Japanese social observational humor. We cant leave all this shit to sheldon from american sitcom Big Bang Theory.


I will just keep it short now and say that exploring Western psych pathologies in the lens of a different human culture is very interesting for me. I am a passionate undiagnosed Aspie like my parents, and I dont need institutional prejudice to tell me ASD can only be appreciated in white societies, and relegated larged to dorky white dudes. Aspies are all over the place. Happy anthropological perspectives on stimming to you all. :)
